newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco negotiators report to White House.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco negotiators report to White House.

text.p: Negotiators for tobacco companies and anti-smoking forces gave the White House an update on their settlement talks on Wednesday and reported that no deal was imminent.

White House deputy counsel Bruce Lindsey met with Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore and several lawyers representing the tobacco companies and plaintiffs who have sued the industry, a White House official said.
Negotiators had met on Sunday and on Monday in Chicago. The talks began about two weeks ago between top industry executives and an array of anti-tobacco leaders.
Published reports have said the industry might pay as much as $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers who fall sick with lung cancer and other diseases.
In return, the tobacco industry would get broad shelter from lawsuits and higher stock market valuations on their thriving tobacco and non-smoking businesses.
"They have not reached a settlement," said a White House official, adding the parties met with Lindsey for about an hour.
The official described the parties as "deep into the negotiations" but that one participant in the White House meeting did not believe a settlement was imminent.
Clinton is closely monitoring the settlement talks to ensure that politically risky steps he took to increase federal oversight of the industry are protected.

Last year he gave broad powers to the federal Food and Drug Administration by approving its contention that nicotine is a drug. That position underpins the FDA's effort to regulate the industry and limit advertising it considers to be aimed at persuading young people to smoke.
The tobacco industry is fighting that regulatory effort in court but there have been reports that the industry negotiators were considering dropping their challenge.

White House officials, while making clear they have not endorsed any settlement proposals, stressed that Clinton could not go along with a settlement that would give tobacco companies blanket protection from future civil lawsuits.
"We've always said we're against blanket immunity," said one official.
Anti-smoking activists are pressuring state attorneys general not to deprive all smokers of the right to sue.
